old: It once described a share or portion of something, a sense now long forgotten.
By the 1600s it had shifted to naming a borrowed fragment of speech or text.
It's built on the same root as the verb "quote," with -ation tacked on.
clues: This noun for a bit of language once had nothing to do with words at all: it named a mere share or portion, tied to counting things out.
Today it names a passage of someone else's exact words repeated in your writing or speech; a citation merely points to the source, while this reproduces the words.
A plumber gives you one as a price estimate before starting a job, and whole books are filled with famous ones, each framed by inverted commas.
